header.title: Tactile Core
header.lede: The internal panel that runs the studio's live games — made calm and cohesive enough for outside studios to run on too.
header.meta: Sole product designer · Internal platform · 2021–25 · Tactile Games

sections.heading: One panel that runs the whole studio
sections.caption: A few of the tools
sections.body:
Tactile Core is the internal platform behind the games — A/B tests, live events, player segments, builds, analytics, support, game config. Dozens of tools, one system.

Every screen here I designed and built myself, between 2021 and 2025.

sections.heading: It started as a drawer of apps that didn't know each other
sections.caption: Navigation, unified
sections.body:
It began as separate tools and spreadsheets on a default Bootstrap theme. It worked — it just didn't hang together. The problem was never the UI. It's utilitarian software.

Making it cohesive was the job. First move: one rail across every tool, plus a switcher to jump between games.

visual.alt: The unified sidebar — every product in one rail

sections.heading: Spin up a test without leaving the page
sections.caption: Create an A/B test
sections.body: Pick the resources to test, add groups, set weights — the whole experiment on one screen. The heavy machinery of an A/B platform, made to feel like filling in a form.

visual.alt: Create A/B Test — test groups, journeys, tracks

sections.heading: A whole test group, judged inside one card
sections.caption: A/B test — one card
sections.body:
Each group is a single card: its weight and split, its journeys and tracks, and its *live* numbers — DAU, ARPDAU, revenue diff — right there. You compare Control against Treatment without leaving the card.

> Dense signal in a small card, without it feeling heavy — the part I enjoy most.

visual.alt: A/B test group card — properties, journeys, and live stats

annotations.label: Live DAU / ARPDAU, in the card

sections.heading: The states nobody screenshots
sections.caption: A/B — states & details
sections.body: A tool is mostly its edges — the empty first-run, the confirm modal, the randomization seed, the in-between card states. Getting these right is what makes it feel finished.

sections.eyebrow: the first thing I got wrong
sections.heading: I built too much design system
sections.caption: Rules > components
sections.body:
I built our Core Design System from scratch — MUI underneath, themed after Untitled UI — and spent too long perfecting components before anyone needed them.

You only need the basics up front: inputs, tables, buttons, type, colour.

> The real work is the patterns and rules — written down from day one. The rules are the product.

sections.heading: Every live event on one timeline
sections.caption: Scheduled features — timeline
sections.body: Scheduled Features puts every event and offer, across every track, on a single timeline with a "today" line through it. Ops sees the whole calendar at once instead of reading a list.

visual.alt: Scheduled Features — timeline of events across tracks

sections.heading: This much JSON, turned into a form
sections.caption: Offer config → editable UI
sections.body: Underneath, an offer is a wall of nested JSON. The tool's job is to make that editable by a human — a form, a timeline, a set of states — instead of a text file someone edits at 2am.

sections.heading: How much a segment overlaps others, at a glance
sections.caption: Segment overlap
sections.body: A small donut per overlap, real percentage beneath. A dense comparison you read in a second — the kind of tiny, information-rich component I could design all day.

sections.heading: One segment, a dozen moments
sections.caption: Segments — the whole surface
sections.body: Details, usage, last-run results, the many-segments case, the two-segments case, the kebab menus, the add-button state. A real tool is the sum of its small, correct moments.

sections.eyebrow: the second thing I got wrong
sections.heading: Consistency isn't the same as sameness
sections.caption: Two tools, intentionally different
sections.body:
I chased uniformity — every tool identical. Wrong. A timeline and a support inbox are different tasks, different mental models, different users.

Only the basics should match — saving, modals, destructive actions, empty states. The rest should be free to be itself.

sections.heading: Stand up a new game — or a new studio
sections.caption: Configure a new game
sections.body: Naming, shortcodes, package + certificate config, team permissions. Enough hand-holding that a brand-new game (or an outside studio) can get running without someone walking them through it.

sections.heading: Built from parts, so it stays consistent
sections.caption: Reusable template parts
sections.body: Permissions, template containers, the fingerprint section — assembled from the same Core parts, so a new flow inherits the system instead of reinventing it.

sections.heading: This whole system, by hand
sections.caption: The whole surface
sections.body: Not a gallery to skim — the point is the surface. One person, one system, this much ground, from 2021 to 2025.

sections.heading: The defaults I inherited became debt
sections.caption: The honest list
sections.body:
Two I'd take back. **Uppercase buttons**, straight from MUI, are now permanent — we tried sentence case and people had gotten used to the shouting. And the **purple** leans too hard in places because we followed MUI's theme instead of our own judgement.

The bigger one: I designed the system but under-taught the *why*. I did it one-on-one when I should have built it into how the whole team thinks. That's the part I do properly now.

visual.art:
WHAT I'D CHANGE

  uppercase BUTTONS ......  MUI default → permanent
  purple everywhere .....   followed the theme, not the need
  taught the "why" 1:1 ..   should've been team-wide

  small defaults you don't decide on
  become decisions anyway.

sections.heading: We set out to make tools usable. We built a product
sections.caption: Where it's headed
sections.body:
No clean number to give — too much changed at once to pin adoption on the redesign, and I'd rather be honest than tidy.

The real outcome was a surprise. The craft — design *and* engineering — got good enough that a games company started seeing itself as a SaaS one. Good internals other studios could run on. That's where it's headed next.

visual.art:
internal tools
        │
        ▼
   [ good enough to sell ]
        │
        ▼
   a games co. → a SaaS co.

   what I'd keep:
   · rules before components
   · teach the system, not just ship it
   · dense can still be calm

footer.headline: One panel to run a studio — good enough to hand to another one.
footer.note: Tactile Core — the studio's internal tooling platform. Designed solo, 2021–25, on a from-scratch Core Design System (MUI base, Untitled-UI-inspired theming).
